newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Jiang to signal continued warm China-Pakistan ties.
newsitem.headline: Jiang to signal continued warm China-Pakistan ties.

text.p: Relations between Pakistan and China will remain close despite Beijing's warming ties with India, Islamabad's arch foe, analysts and diplomats said on Thursday.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to India that was due to start on Thursday has created some rumblings of worry that Delhi is drawing Beijing away from Pakistan, with which it has had close diplomatic and military ties for three decades.

But political analysts, diplomats and officials said such concerns were exaggerated and Jiang's four-day visit to Pakistan starting on Sunday would symbolise the enduring nature of Beijing's ties to Islamabad.
"This is a relationship in which we have full trust," Foreign Ministry spokesman Khalid Salim told reporters.
"We are certain that any arrangements China may make with India will not be against the interests of Pakistan."

Concerns have been raised in the Pakistani press that possible agreement on troop reductions along the Indo-Chinese border, where the two countries fought a brief border war in 1962, would allow India to concentrate more on Pakistan.

Some columnists have suggested that a weakening of ties with China at a time when attempts to foster good relations with Iran have broken down over the backing of different sides in the Afghan civil war could be a major setback for Islamabad.

Relations between India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, are still poor. But political analysts and diplomats said they agreed with Salim that Beijing's ties with Islamabad would not be affected by any agreements Jiang signed in Delhi.
"This is not a triangular relationship. Everybody gains if China's relations are warm with Delhi because I don't see any way that will affect Pakistan-China ties," said one diplomat.
"There is no cause for concern. We are not at all worried," Pakistani former army chief Mirza Aslam Beg told Reuters.
"There has been no decline in our relations with China and now it's a question of consolidation."

Jiang will meet President Farooq Leghari and top members of the caretaker government he installed earlier this month after dismissing prime minister Benazir Bhutto's three-year-old administration on charges of corruption and incompetence.
Pakistan's political turmoil was something of a problem, Beg said.

"Our relations have developed over a long time and a change of faces doesn't make any difference in the long term, but with the changes at the top in both places we do need to develop contacts between the new leaderships," he said.
Officials said Jiang, who will be accompanied by Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and Foreign Trade Minister Wu Yi, was unlikely to discuss significant policy issues.

But his visit to the country where he once worked as a plant manager on a Chinese aid project and where he has many personal friends, according to officials, would be a major symbol of warm ties between the two nations.

Officials said he would address the Pakistani Senate -- but not the Indian upper house in what diplomats said was an important signal of the primacy of Beijing's relations with Pakistan in South Asia.
